day-1.t: Day 1 — Turn a wish into a scope

b.v: Today's goal

v: Write a one-page scope for a real project
List what is inside and what is outside
Agree what done means before any work starts

b.v: About 20 minutes. Keep our running example in your head: Rise & Shine Bakes, a home bakery in Rawalpindi, opening a small counter in Saddar in 12 weeks.

Nadia owns Rise & Shine Bakes. She sells cakes from home on WhatsApp and wants a counter in Saddar. Her wish is one sentence. A project is that sentence turned into boundaries: what we will do, what we will not do, by when, for how much, and how we will know it worked. Without boundaries, every conversation ends in an argument about whether something was included.
1) Write the six lines of a scope statement
You do not need a template with twenty headings. Six lines cover it, and one page is the right length because people actually read one page.

Write these six lines for Nadia's project:|Purpose: open a 250 sq ft cake counter in Saddar so walk-in customers can buy the same cakes we sell on WhatsApp|Deliverable: a fitted counter, a menu, a trained person, and a working daily cash routine|Out of scope: a second kitchen, a website, delivery riders|Budget: Rs 850,000 including one month rent advance|Deadline: counter open by 15 January|Success: Rs 60,000 of counter sales in the first full month with no stock-outs of the six best sellers
2) Make the out-of-scope list loud

The out-of-scope list is the most valuable part of the page. It is the thing you point at in week seven when someone casually asks for delivery riders too. Write it in plain words a non-project person understands.

v: In scope = shop fit-out, licence paperwork, stock, one staff hire, menu, opening promotion
Out of scope = new kitchen equipment, delivery bikes, a second staff member, website, catering contracts
Out of scope does not mean never = it means not in this project, and we will discuss it as a new project
If it is not on the page = it is out of scope, and adding it needs a written change

b.v: The most common beginner mistake is agreeing to a deadline before listing the work. A date agreed in a happy first meeting becomes a promise you cannot keep. List the work first, then set the date from the work.
3) Define done in numbers
Done must be measurable, or the project never closes. The test is simple: could two different people look at the result and agree whether it passed?

v: Weak: the shop looks good
Strong: counter fitted, six best sellers in stock, one person trained on the till and the cash book, first sale recorded
Weak: customers know about us
Strong: 300 flyers given out and 150 WhatsApp broadcast messages sent to past customers in week 12

b.v: Practice

Take one thing you personally want to finish in the next two months, at work or in your own business. Write the six lines on paper, and force yourself to write at least three items in out of scope. If you cannot think of three, you have not decided what you are not doing yet.

day-2.t: Day 2 — Break the work down until it is obvious

b.v: Today's goal

v: Split a project into work packages
Stop at the right size of task
Find the missing work before it finds you

b.v: About 25 minutes. Do it on paper or in a notes app, not in fancy software.

A work breakdown structure sounds grand. It is just a list in layers: the project, then its main chunks, then the tasks inside each chunk. The purpose is to see the whole job at once, because hidden work is what destroys deadlines.
1) Three layers is enough
Project, then work package, then task. Keep the task small enough that you can say whether it is done today. If a task has the word and in it twice, it is too big.

Break down Nadia's counter project:|Layer 1: the project, counter opening|Layer 2: five packages — legal, premises, fit-out, stock and suppliers, people and launch|Layer 3: tasks inside each package. Example inside premises: agree rent, sign agreement, pay advance, get electricity connection transferred|Keep going until each task is one person, one action, under three days

v: Legal = shop registration, food licence application, tax registration if required
Premises = rent agreed, agreement signed, advance paid, utilities in place
Fit-out = counter built, shelving, fridge, signage, lighting
Stock and suppliers = packaging, ingredients, six best sellers costed, first order placed
People and launch = hire, train, menu printed, flyers, opening day plan

b.v: 2) The task size test
A task you cannot finish in three days is not a task, it is a package pretending to be one. Big tasks hide problems until the last week, when there is no time left.

v: Good task = call the signage shop and confirm price and 5-day delivery
Too big = sort out the signage
Good task = order 500 flyers, approve proof, pay Rs 6,500
Too big = marketing
Rule of thumb = if it needs more than one sentence to describe, split it

b.v: Do not break the work down alone and then hand it out. The person who will do the task sees steps you cannot see. A ten-minute conversation with the carpenter prevents a two-week surprise.
3) Hunt for the missing 20 per cent
Every first breakdown misses roughly a fifth of the work, always the same kind: approvals, waiting time, and cleaning up. Add a line for each before you estimate dates.

v: Approval = who signs, how long they take, what they need to see
Waiting = delivery lead time, bank processing, licence office days
Rework = the first version of the menu, the sign, or the layout will change
Handover = training, keys, passwords, supplier contacts written down

b.v: Practice

Break your project down to at least 25 tasks across no more than six packages. Then read the list and circle every task that involves someone outside your control. Those circles are your future delays, and tomorrow you give each one an owner and a date.
Today's goal

v: Set four or five milestones, not forty
Give every task exactly one owner
Build a date chain that survives one delay

b.v: About 20 minutes. Bring your task list from Day 2.

A milestone is a date when something visible becomes true. Not an activity: a result. Owners are the single name next to each task. Both exist for one reason, so that in week six nobody can say they thought someone else was doing it.
1) Choose milestones you could photograph
A good milestone is provable. If you cannot describe what you would see, hear or count on that date, it is a phase, not a milestone.

Set Nadia's five milestones:|Week 2: rent agreement signed and advance paid|Week 5: shop empty and fit-out started|Week 8: counter, fridge and signage installed|Week 10: licence in hand and first stock delivered|Week 12: one trained person serving, opening day done

v: Four to six milestones = right for a 12-week project
One milestone per two to three weeks = keeps attention without noise
Every milestone needs a date and a name
A missed milestone triggers a conversation, not a silent slide

b.v: 2) One owner per task, always
Shared ownership means no ownership. Write one name. Other people can help, but one person answers for it being done, and that person must know they own it out loud.

v: Owner = the person who reports whether it is done, not always the person doing the work
Support = listed separately, never in the owner column
Nadia's fit-out owner = the carpenter, with Nadia supporting on decisions
Licence owner = Nadia herself, because only she can sign the papers

b.v: Never write two names in one owner cell to keep everyone happy. It guarantees that both wait for the other, and you find out three days before opening.
3) Chain the dates so one delay does not kill the project
Some tasks must follow others: you cannot install a fridge before the wiring. Others only look sequential and can overlap. Knowing the difference is the whole skill of scheduling.

Build the chain:|List every task that must finish before another can start|Mark the true dependencies only. Sign before fit-out, yes. Menu before flyers, yes|Overlap anything independent. Training can happen while signage is being made|Add a buffer before the opening date, not after it. Two weeks is sensible for a first shop|Work backwards from the opening date to see whether the chain fits
Practice

Write your five milestones with dates and one owner each. Then take the last milestone and work backwards task by task. If the arithmetic does not fit inside your deadline, cut scope now. Cutting in week one is a decision. Cutting in week eleven is a crisis.

day-4.t: Day 4 — One tracker everyone can see

b.v: Today's goal

v: Build a six-column tracker you will actually update
Keep the tracker as the single truth
Report progress with a number, not a feeling

b.v: About 20 minutes. A spreadsheet or even a paper sheet on the wall works. The tool does not matter.
Most trackers die in week two because they have forty columns and one person updates them privately. The one that survives is short, shared, and updated in the weekly meeting while people watch.
1) Six columns are enough
Every extra column is a place to lie or forget. These six carry everything a small project needs.

v: Task = one action, short enough to read in the row
Owner = one name
Due = the date it must be done
Status = Not started, In progress, Blocked, Done. Only these four
Next step = the single next action, written as a verb
Note = what is stuck and who must unblock it

b.v: Build it in 15 minutes:|Open a spreadsheet and type the six headings in row one|Paste your tasks in the Task column|Add owner and due date for every row|Leave status as Not started|Freeze the header row and share the link with everyone named|Put a filter on Status so Blocked items can be seen in one click
2) Make Blocked do real work

Blocked is the most useful status in the list. A blocked task is waiting for a person or a paper, and it cannot move without help. Anything blocked for more than three days is your job as the project lead, not the owner's.

v: Blocked by a person = you call that person today
Blocked by a payment = you release the payment today
Blocked by a decision = you ask the decision maker one clear question with two options
Never leave a task In progress for two weeks without touching it. That is a hidden Blocked

b.v: Do not run two trackers, one for the boss and one for the team. They drift apart within a month and then every meeting is spent arguing about which one is right. One tracker, one link, everyone edits the same file.
3) Turn the tracker into a progress number
People believe percentages that are calculated, not guessed. Count tasks, and count milestones. Two numbers are enough for any upward report.

Calculate honestly:|Count tasks marked Done and divide by total tasks. That is task progress|Count milestones passed and compare with milestones planned by today|If task progress is 80 per cent but milestones are 2 of 5, the project is not 80 per cent done|Report the milestone number, because that is the one that matters
Practice

Build the six-column tracker with at least 20 real tasks. Mark what is genuinely done. Then look at the gap between your task percentage and your milestone percentage. Write one sentence explaining the gap. That sentence is the most useful thing you will produce this week.

day-5.t: Day 5 — The weekly meeting that decides things

b.v: Today's goal

v: Run a 25-minute meeting with a fixed shape
Separate information from decisions
End every meeting with owners and dates

b.v: About 20 minutes. If you already run a weekly meeting, bring your last agenda.

Most project meetings are status theatre: eight people read out what everyone already read in the tracker, then the real problem is discussed in the corridor afterwards. A good meeting is short, skips the parts people can read, and spends its time on decisions.
1) Send the tracker before, not during
If people can read the status, do not read it aloud. Circulate the tracker one hour before and ask everyone to add a next step. The meeting then starts with what is stuck.

v: Before = tracker updated by each owner, one line on what is blocked
During = only blocked items, decisions, and changes to dates
After = three lines in WhatsApp: decisions, owners, dates
Never = a round-the-table update that takes 20 minutes

b.v: 2) The 25-minute shape
A fixed shape stops the meeting drifting. Same order every week, and the clock is visible to everyone.

Run it like this:|Minutes 0 to 3: read the three numbers. Tasks done, milestones passed, days to opening|Minutes 3 to 13: blocked items only. Owner speaks, no history, just the block and what they need|Minutes 13 to 22: decisions. Each one written as a sentence with a name and a date|Minutes 22 to 25: confirm the three most important things for next week|Send the three-line summary in WhatsApp within ten minutes
3) Write decisions, not discussions
A decision is a sentence someone can act on. If the sentence could start with we discussed, it is not a decision. This single habit makes a project feel calm.

v: Bad = we talked about the signage size
Good = signage will be 4 ft by 2 ft, Imran orders it by Thursday, Rs 18,000 maximum
Bad = everyone agreed the menu needs work
Good = menu has 12 items, Imran sends the design Friday, Nadia approves by Monday

b.v: Do not invite everyone to every meeting. Each extra person adds a reason to be polite instead of direct. Invite the owners of blocked items and the person who can approve money. Everyone else reads the three-line summary.
Practice

Write the agenda for your next weekly meeting using the 25-minute shape, and prepare the three numbers. Then write the three-line WhatsApp summary you expect to send at the end. Doing this before the meeting is what keeps it short.

day-6.t: Day 6 — Risks and dependencies before they bite

b.v: Today's goal

v: List the five risks that could actually stop you
Give each a trigger and a response
Track dependencies outside your control

b.v: About 20 minutes. Be pessimistic on purpose. This is the one lesson where worry is productive.

A risk is something that might happen. A dependency is something you need from someone else. Both are ordinary, and both are cheap to handle early and expensive to handle late. The point is not to predict the future, it is to decide now what you will do if the bad thing happens.
1) Five risks, scored simply
Score each risk as high, medium or low for how likely it is and how bad it would be. Anything high on both gets an action today. Anything low on both gets written down and ignored.

Build the risk list for the counter project:|Licence takes longer than expected. Likely: medium. Impact: high. Response: apply in week 1, keep a copy of every receipt, ask for the officer's name|Carpenter delivers late. Likely: medium. Impact: high. Response: written delivery date, part payment on delivery|First month sales below Rs 60,000. Likely: medium. Impact: medium. Response: keep two weeks of cash reserve, plan an opening offer|Staff member leaves after training. Likely: low. Impact: high. Response: write the routine down, train a family member as backup|Ingredient price rises. Likely: medium. Impact: low. Response: cost the menu again before printing
2) Give every risk a trigger
A trigger is the observable sign that the risk is happening. Without a trigger, you notice problems only when they are already a crisis.

v: Trigger for the licence = no response by day 20
Trigger for the carpenter = no visit on the agreed day
Trigger for slow sales = under Rs 12,000 in week two
When a trigger fires = you act on the planned response the same day, no re-discussion

b.v: Do not keep a risk list you never open. Ten risks in a file nobody reads is worse than three risks written on the meeting agenda every week. Put the top three on the weekly agenda permanently.
3) Dependencies are other people's calendars
The tasks most likely to slip are the ones you cannot do yourself. For each dependency, write what you need, from whom, by when, and what you will do if it does not arrive.

v: Electricity connection = from the landlord and the utility office. Ask in week 1
Licence = from the local authority. Ask what documents they need before you queue
Fridge delivery = from the supplier. Confirm the date in writing, not on a call
Family approval on spending = from your partner or father. Agree the limit before you need it

b.v: Practice

Write five risks for your project in the format: risk, likelihood, impact, trigger, response. Then write three dependencies with a name and a date in each. Put the top three risks on next week's agenda and keep them there until they are closed.

day-7.t: Day 7 — Saying no to scope creep without a fight

b.v: Today's goal

v: Recognise the three ways scope grows
Use a script that keeps the relationship
Run a simple change note when the answer is yes

b.v: About 20 minutes. Think of one request you said yes to and later regretted.

Scope creep is not one big outrageous request. It is twenty small reasonable ones, each of which takes two days. By the end, the deadline is impossible and everyone remembers the deadline but nobody remembers the twenty agreements. The fix is a habit, not a personality.
1) The three ways scope grows
Name the pattern and you can answer it in seconds.

v: The small favour = can you also add delivery? Small, reasonable, and it needs a bike, a rider and insurance
The quality creep = can we use imported tiles instead? Same scope, double the cost
The moving target = actually let us do the website first. Different project dressed as the same one

b.v: 2) One script, three sentences
Say no to the request, not to the person. Then offer the real choice: more time, more money, or a smaller project. People accept that far more easily than a flat refusal.

Use this script word for word:|Yes, that is a good idea and I can see why you want it.|It is not in the plan we agreed, so it is not in the date or the budget.|We have two options: add it and move opening to March, or keep January and do it as a separate small project in February. Which do you prefer?

Never say let me see what I can do. It sounds helpful and it means yes. The other person hears yes, plans around yes, and blames you when it does not happen. A clear no today is kinder than a quiet failure in week ten.
3) When you do say yes, write it down
Some changes are worth making. Accepting them is fine, as long as the trade is written and agreed in the same conversation.

Write a change note in five lines:|What is being added, in one sentence|Why, in one sentence|Extra cost in rupees, and extra days|What moves as a result. Either the date, or another item is dropped|Both names and the date, sent on WhatsApp so there is a record

v: A change note is five lines in WhatsApp, not a form
One change note per change. Do not batch them into a vague summary later
If the change is free, still write it. The record is the point
Dropping something else is the cheapest way to say yes without moving the date

b.v: Practice

Write out the three-sentence script in your own words on a note you can see on your phone. Then take one pending request on your project and answer it using the script today, offering the trade instead of a plain yes or no.
Today's goal

v: Write a status report a busy owner can read in 60 seconds
Report bad news early in a way that keeps trust
Ask for decisions instead of sympathy

b.v: About 20 minutes. Write the report for a real project, even if nobody asked for it.

Owners and investors do not want a story, they want to know three things: is it on track, what is stuck, and what do you need from me. Most people report effort instead of position, which is why the owner keeps asking for updates.
1) The five-line weekly report
Five lines, same order every week. After a month, the reader trusts it because the shape never changes and the numbers are real.

Write it like this:|Status: Amber. Two milestones done of five planned|Done this week: rent agreement signed, advance paid, carpenter booked|Next week: fit-out starts Monday, licence file submitted|Stuck: electricity connection needs the landlord's signature. Chasing Thursday|Need from you: approve Rs 45,000 extra for wiring, decision by Friday

v: Green = on track, no decision needed
Amber = one thing is at risk, a decision is needed this week
Red = the date or budget will not hold without a change
Never report Green for three weeks and then Red. That is the pattern that loses trust

b.v: 2) Deliver bad news with a plan attached
Bad news alone creates panic. Bad news with a plan and a choice creates confidence. Always bring the problem, the cause in one line, two options and your recommendation.

Structure the message:|The problem, stated plainly in one sentence|The cause, without blaming a person by name|Two options with cost and date impact|Your recommendation and why|The decision you need, and by when

Do not hide a slipping date to avoid an uncomfortable call. The owner will find out at the opening, and by then the only thing they remember is that you knew. Early bad news is treated as professionalism. Late bad news is treated as dishonesty.
3) Translate activity into money and time
Owners think in rupees and days. Convert your work into those units and your reports get read.

v: Not useful = 12 tasks completed this week
Useful = fit-out is 40 per cent paid, on schedule for week 8, Rs 12,000 under budget
Not useful = supplier coordination ongoing
Useful = fridge arrives Monday, three days late, no effect on opening date

b.v: Practice

Write this week's five-line report for your project, using a real colour status. Then write one bad-news message using the five-part structure, even if you do not need to send it yet. Having the words ready is what makes you send it early next time.
Today's goal

v: Build a go-live checklist that catches the boring failures
Hand over to the person who will run it
Plan the first two weeks after launch

b.v: About 20 minutes. Write the checklist for a real launch, even a small one.

Projects rarely fail in the big obvious way. They fail because the card machine was never tested, the change float was never arranged, and the person who built everything is on a bus to Lahore on day one. Launch day is a checklist job, not a creative job.
1) The go-live checklist
Walk the actual customer path yourself, in order, before opening. Every step is a chance to find a small disaster while it is still cheap.

Walk the path for Nadia's counter one day before opening:|Stand outside. Is the sign lit and readable from across the road?|Walk in. Is the counter clean, is the fridge at temperature?|Read the menu from where a customer stands. Are all 12 items in stock?|Pay for one item yourself, in cash, and record it in the cash book|Pay with the card machine or wallet and confirm the money actually arrived|Ask a stranger to buy something and say nothing. Watch where they get confused|Lock up and check keys, lights, shutter and cash

v: Cash float = small notes and coins counted and recorded
Contact list = supplier, electrician, landlord, licence office, all on one sheet
Backup = who covers if the trained person is sick on day two
Numbers = the daily sales figure written in one place, every day, from day one

b.v: 2) Hand over, do not walk away
Handover is a document and a conversation, not a goodbye. If the routine lives only in your head, the project is not finished, you have just moved the dependency to yourself.

Hand over properly:|Write the daily routine on one page: open, clean, count stock, serve, record sales, close|Walk through it together twice, once with you doing it, once with them doing it|Write down passwords, supplier numbers and who to call when something breaks|Agree what they may decide alone and what needs your call|Set a daily 5-minute check for the first two weeks
Do not hand over on the busiest day. Launch on a quiet weekday if you can, so mistakes happen in front of six customers instead of sixty. The first day is for learning, not for maximum sales.
3) Plan the first two weeks after launch
Launch is a milestone, not the end. The project is only stable when the routine runs without you. Give it two weeks of attention, then step back.

v: Week one = be present daily, watch, fix small things, do not redesign
Week two = visit every second day, check the numbers, ask what is annoying
Decide the three things that need changing, and change only those
Then close the project and write the review

b.v: Practice

Write your own go-live checklist with at least 12 items in the order a customer experiences them. Then write the one-page routine for whoever will run it. If you cannot fit the routine on one page, you have not simplified it enough.

day-10.t: Day 10 — The post-project review that pays for itself

b.v: Today's goal

v: Run a 45-minute review without blame
Compare plan with reality using numbers
Leave three written changes for the next project

b.v: About 20 minutes. Do this within two weeks of finishing, before memory softens.

A review is not a complaint session and not a celebration. It is the only mechanism by which a business gets better at projects. Do it once per project, write three things, and the second project is measurably easier than the first.
1) Compare plan with reality, in numbers
Start with facts, because opinions arrive fast and loud. Four numbers tell you almost everything.

v: Planned date versus actual date, in days
Planned budget versus actual spend, in rupees
Planned scope versus what was actually delivered
Success measure versus the real result, for example Rs 60,000 target versus Rs 47,000 actual in month one

b.v: Fill the four numbers first:|Opening planned 15 January, actual 29 January. Fourteen days late|Budget Rs 850,000, actual Rs 903,000. Over by Rs 53,000, mostly wiring and signage|Scope delivered as planned, except the menu went from 12 to 9 items|First month sales Rs 47,000 against a Rs 60,000 target
2) Ask four questions, in this order
The order matters. You start with what worked, because otherwise people defend themselves and you learn nothing. Then you move to causes, not names.

Ask and write answers:|What worked that we should repeat?|What went wrong, and what caused it? Describe the cause, not the person|Where did we get lucky? Luck is not a plan|What will we do differently next time, stated as an action?

Do not turn the review into a search for who to blame. The moment one person is blamed, everyone else stops telling the truth, and next project you will hear about problems even later. Blame the plan, fix the process.
3) Leave three changes, not thirty
A review that produces thirty recommendations produces zero changes. Choose three, write them as rules, and put them where the next project will see them.

v: Rule 1 = every task that depends on an outside supplier gets a written delivery date
Rule 2 = 10 per cent of the budget is held as contingency and not spent in week one
Rule 3 = menu and price list are approved before the print order is placed
Keep the rules in one file called How we run projects. Add one per project, never rewrite

b.v: Practice

Run the review on a project you have finished, even a small one. Fill the four numbers, answer the four questions in writing, and choose exactly three rules for your How we run projects file. Then close the tracker and archive it, so the next project starts clean.
